citations.quote: Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network from $[0,1]^d$ to $\mathbb R^r$ is a finite acyclic feedforward computation graph with $d$ input coordinates, hidden units applying $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to affine combinations of earlier unit values, and $r$ affine output units. Edges may skip layers. Its depth is the maximum number of layers met on an input-to-output path, counting the input and output layers, so a network with one hidden layer has depth $3$. Its computation units are its hidden and output units; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. The number of each quantity counts scalar entries, including zero entries only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network is the specialization in which edges join consecutive layers and every such edge is present.

derivations.claim: Before any hidden layer, the input is affine on $I$. Suppose all values through layer $\ell-1$ are affine on each of $M$ subintervals. On any one such interval, every preactivation in layer $\ell$ is affine, and each has at most one zero unless it is identically zero. The at most $n_\ell$ zeros divide that interval into at most $n_\ell+1$ subintervals on each of which all ReLU outputs are affine.

Induction over the hidden layers gives at most $\prod_{\ell=1}^H(n_\ell+1)$ intervals; the affine output adds no breakpoints. For $H\ge1$, AM–GM gives $\prod(n_\ell+1)\le(1+H^{-1}\sum n_\ell)^H=(1+U/H)^H$. With no hidden layer the output is affine on the entire interval.

citations.quote: Let $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ and define $\tau(x)=2\rho(x)-4\rho(x-1/2)$ for $x\in[0,1]$. For each integer $q\ge0$, $\tau^q$ is affine and maps bijectively onto $[0,1]$ on each of the $2^q$ dyadic intervals $[j2^{-q},(j+1)2^{-q}]$, with slope of magnitude $2^q$. It is computed on $[0,1]$ by a ReLU network with $2q$ hidden units, $q$ hidden layers, and $O(q+1)$ weights; its depth, counting input and output layers, is $q+2$.

derivations.claim: Let $I_q$ be the linear interpolant of $x^2$ at the dyadic nodes $j2^{-q}$. On each interval of $I_{q-1}$, the difference $I_{q-1}-I_q$ is zero at its endpoints and has height $4^{-q}$ at the midpoint. By [F1], $\tau^q$ is the unit tent on each such interval, so $I_{q-1}-I_q=4^{-q}\tau^q$. Since $I_0(x)=x$, telescoping gives $I_m(x)=x-\sum_{q=1}^m4^{-q}\tau^q(x)$.

On a dyadic interval $[a,b]$ of length $2^{-m}$, linear interpolation of $x^2$ has error $(x-a)(b-x)$, whose maximum is $(b-a)^2/4=4^{-(m+1)}$. Choose $m$ with $4^{-(m+1)}\le\delta$. Then $I_m$ approximates $x^2$ within $\delta$ and $I_m(0)=0$.

Compute the $m$ iterates in parallel-stage form from [F1] and combine their outputs with the affine sum in step 1.1. The resulting network has $O(m+1)$ units, weights, and depth, and $m\le C'(1+\log(1/\delta))$ by the choice of $m$. Taking $Q_\delta=I_m$ proves the claim.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in [[lem-pointwise-potential-bound-for-compactly-supported-smooth-functions]]. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Fix a nonnegative
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ of unit mass with
$\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$, put
$\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and define the
interior mollification
$$u_\varepsilon(x)=(\rho_\varepsilon*\widetilde u)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde u(y)\,\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy,$$
where $\widetilde u$ is a representative of $u$ extended by zero to
$\mathbb R^n$. Then $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every
open $U\subset\subset\Omega$; equivalently $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in
$W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. The exponent $p=1$ is included, and
no assertion about density or convergence in the $W^{k,\infty}$ norm is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

derivations.claim: For each $|\alpha|<n$, $D^\alpha f\in W^{1,\infty}(Q)$ by [F1], since its first weak derivatives are among the derivatives of $f$ of order at most $n$. By [F1], choose their Lipschitz representatives; their Lipschitz constants are at most $\sqrt d$, because each coordinate weak derivative has essential supremum at most $1$. Since $Q$ has finite measure and all derivatives of order at most $n-1$ are essentially bounded, the same weak-derivative identities give $f\in W^{n-1,1}(Q)$. By [A1] and [F2], Countable Choice holds, and the interior mollification theorem applies with $k=n-1$ and $p=1$. For every compact segment in $Q$, convolution of each Lipschitz representative differs from it uniformly by at most $\sqrt d$ times the mollifier radius, so the mollified derivatives through order $n-1$ converge uniformly there.

For an interior grid center $a_m$ and interior $x$, choose the mollifier radius smaller than the distance from their segment to $\partial Q$. By [F3], $D^\alpha f_\delta=\rho_\delta*D^\alpha f$ on that segment; nonnegativity and unit mass of $\rho_\delta$ imply $|D^\alpha f_\delta|\le\|D^\alpha f\|_\infty\le1$ for $|\alpha|=n$. The one-variable Taylor formula applied to $t\mapsto f_\delta(a_m+t(x-a_m))$ therefore gives remainder at most $\frac1{n!}\sup_t|\frac{d^n}{dt^n}f_\delta(a_m+t(x-a_m))|\le C(d,n)\|x-a_m\|_\infty^n$, since $\sum_i|x_i-a_{m,i}|\le d\|x-a_m\|_\infty$. Passing to the uniform limits from step 1.1 proves the estimate for interior points. Approximate any boundary grid center and any boundary input by interior points; the Lipschitz extensions of all coefficients and the finite Taylor polynomial are continuous, so the same estimate holds on the closed cube.

The one-dimensional hats sum to $1$ on each grid interval, so their tensor products satisfy $\sum_m\phi_m=1$ on the cube; at most $2^d$ are nonzero at any point, and each nonzero term has $\|x-a_m\|_\infty\le1/N$. Therefore $|f(x)-g_N(x)|\le\sum_{m:\phi_m(x)>0}\phi_m(x)C(d,n)N^{-n}=C(d,n)N^{-n}$. Each $u_\alpha$ and each hat is continuous on the closed cube, so the finite sum $g_N$ extends continuously there.

For each center $a_m$, write its Taylor polynomial as a finite sum of monomials in the scaled variables $z_i=N(x_i-a_{m,i})$, multiplied by coefficients $D^\alpha f(a_m)N^{-|\alpha|}/\alpha!$. On the support of $\phi_m$, $|z_i|\le1$, and all coefficients are bounded by a constant depending only on $d,n$. The hat $\phi_m$ is the product of $d$ one-dimensional ReLU hats, since $|z|=\rho(z)+\rho(-z)$ and $u_+=\rho(u)$. There are only a number depending on $d,n$ of products and summands. Choose the error of each product operation to be $\eta/C(d,n)$; inductively, multiplying by a factor of magnitude at most $1$ adds at most that error to the previous product error, and summing the finitely many terms multiplies it by at most another $C(d,n)$. Thus the monomial sum and then its product with the hat have term error at most $\eta$. Every intermediate input stays in a fixed bounded interval depending only on $d,n$, and the final product is exactly zero whenever any hat factor vanishes, by [F2]. The resulting subnetwork has $O_{d,n}(1+\log(1/\eta))$ weights, units, and depth.

At any $x$, at most $2^d$ of the exact hats are nonzero by [F1], and the constructed approximate term is zero outside the same support. Thus summing all local subnetworks gives a network $\Phi_f$ with $\|g_N-\Phi_f\|_\infty\le2^d\eta$. Choose $\eta=\varepsilon/2^{d+1}$. Then the triangle inequality and step 1.1 give $\|f-\Phi_f\|_\infty\le\varepsilon$.

The local polynomial degree and number of terms depend only on $d,n$, while the grid size depends only on $N$. All local subnetworks have depth $O_{d,n}(1+\log(1/\eta))$ and size of the same order; they run in parallel and their outputs are summed affinely. Hence the total depth is $O_{d,n}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ and the total weights and units are $O_{d,n}(N^d(1+\log(1/\varepsilon)))=O_{d,n}(\varepsilon^{-d/n}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$. The edge pattern depends on $N,d,n,\varepsilon$ but not on $f$; only Taylor coefficients and output weights depend on $f$.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in [[lem-pointwise-potential-bound-for-compactly-supported-smooth-functions]]. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network from $[0,1]^d$ to $\mathbb R^r$ is a finite acyclic feedforward computation graph with $d$ input coordinates, hidden units applying $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to affine combinations of earlier unit values, and $r$ affine output units. Edges may skip layers. Its depth is the maximum number of layers met on an input-to-output path, counting the input and output layers, so a network with one hidden layer has depth $3$. Its computation units are its hidden and output units; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. The number of each quantity counts scalar entries, including zero entries only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network is the specialization in which edges join consecutive layers and every such edge is present.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2], the Countable Choice convention in [F1] holds. Choose the Lipschitz representative on $(0,1)$ and extend it uniquely to $[0,1]$: values along any sequence approaching an endpoint are Cauchy and any two such limits agree by the Lipschitz bound. The continuous representative satisfies $|f|\le1$ everywhere, since any interior value with modulus greater than $1$ would by continuity violate the almost-everywhere bound on an interval of positive measure. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer and let $f_1$ linearly interpolate $f$ at $t/T$, $0\le t\le T$. Then $f_1$ is $1$-Lipschitz, and $f_2=f-f_1$ vanishes at every grid endpoint and is $2$-Lipschitz. Indeed, both summands are $1$-Lipschitz.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $\Gamma$ be the set of piecewise-linear functions on the grid $r/m$, $0\le r\le m$, with endpoint values zero and successive increments in $\{-2/m,0,2/m\}$. Thus $|\Gamma|\le3^m$. For each coarse interval $I_t=[t/T,(t+1)/T)$, rescale $g_t(y)=Tf_2((t+y)/T)$. This function is $2$-Lipschitz and vanishes at both endpoints. Quantize each node value down to the nearest multiple of $2/m$; adjacent quantized values differ by one of the three allowed increments. At a fraction $\theta$ of a grid subinterval, a $2$-Lipschitz function differs from its endpoint chord by at most $4\theta(1-\theta)/m\le1/m$; quantizing both endpoint values changes that chord by at most $2/m$. Hence some $\gamma_t\in\Gamma$ satisfies $\sup_{x\in I_t}|f_2(x)-T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)|\le3/(Tm)$.

Define the discontinuous selector $\chi(z)=z$ for $0\le z<1$ and $0$ otherwise. For $x\in[0,1)$, exactly the index $t$ with $x\in I_t$ has $\chi(Tx-t)=Tx-t$; all other terms vanish. Therefore $$\widetilde f_2(x)=\frac1T\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma\!\left(\sum_{t:\gamma_t=\gamma}\chi(Tx-t)\right)$$ equals the local interpolant $T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)$ and has error at most $3/(Tm)$. If $s_{\gamma,r}$ is the slope of $\gamma$ on $[r/m,(r+1)/m]$, then its zero value at $0$ gives $$\gamma(z)=s_{\gamma,0}\rho(z)+\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}(s_{\gamma,r}-s_{\gamma,r-1})\rho(z-r/m),\qquad 0\le z\le1,$$ by matching the initial slope and each slope jump. This uses $m$ ReLU hinges. The cache is a depth-five mixed-gate network with $O(T+m3^m)$ units and weights: $T$ selector units, at most $3^m$ grouped sums, $m3^m$ ReLU hinge units, and an affine output. For the coarse interpolant, set $s_t=T(f((t+1)/T)-f(t/T))$ for $0\le t<T$; then $$f_1(x)=f(0)+s_0\rho(x)+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(s_t-s_{t-1})\rho(x-t/T)$$ on $[0,1]$. This slope-jump identity has $T$ ReLU units and one affine output, so $f_1$ is a depth-three ReLU network of size $O(T)$.

Replace each discontinuous selector by $$\chi_\delta(z)=\rho(z)-\delta^{-1}\rho(z-(1-\delta))+(\delta^{-1}-1)\rho(z-1).$$ This continuous piecewise-linear function agrees with $\chi$ on $[0,1-\delta]$, decreases linearly to zero on $[1-\delta,1]$, and is zero outside $[0,1]$. Let $\varphi_\delta$ be the piecewise-linear tent that is zero outside $[0,1-\delta]$, rises from $0$ to $1$ on $[0,\delta]$, equals $1$ on $[\delta,1-2\delta]$, and falls to $0$ on $[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$. Its four slope jumps give a representation by at most four ReLU hinges as in step 3.1. Put $\Phi_\delta(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\varphi_\delta(Tx-t)$; this comb is a ReLU spline with $O(T)$ units and weights. Replacing the $T$ selectors by three ReLU units each and adding the comb keeps the cache size $O(T+m3^m)$ independently of $\delta$.

Let $\widetilde f_{2,\delta}$ be the cache network using $\chi_\delta$, and set $$f_{2,\delta}(x)=\rho(\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)+2\Phi_\delta(x)-1)-\rho(2\Phi_\delta(x)-1).$$ At most one selector is nonzero at any $x$, its value lies in $[0,1]$, and each rescaled $\gamma_t$ vanishes at both endpoints and is $2$-Lipschitz; hence $|\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)|\le1$. On each plateau where $\Phi_\delta=1$, the selector is unchanged and the gate outputs the cache. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, the two ReLU terms cancel. On the transition strips $y\in[0,\delta]$ or $y\in[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$ in a coarse coordinate $y=Tx-t$, $\chi_\delta(y)=\chi(y)$, so the cache equals the continuous piecewise-linear spline $\widetilde f_2$ from step 3.1. For $0\le p\le1$, the map $a\mapsto\rho(a+2p-1)-\rho(2p-1)$ is $1$-Lipschitz and vanishes at $a=0$, hence its output has modulus at most $|a|$. Every point where $0<\Phi_\delta<1$ is within $2\delta/T$ of a coarse endpoint; both $f_2$ and $\widetilde f_2$ vanish there and are $2$-Lipschitz, so on those strips $|f_2-f_{2,\delta}|\le8\delta/T$. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, $f_{2,\delta}=0$ and $|f_2|\le4\delta/T$, which is also within this bound. On plateaus the quantization error is at most $3/(Tm)$ by step 2.1. Thus $$\|f_2-f_{2,\delta}\|_\infty\le 8\delta/T+3/(Tm).$$ The two final ReLU preactivations absorb the former affine cache output, followed by a shared affine output, so depth increases from five to six; complexity remains $O(T+m3^m)$.

Choose $m=\lceil\tfrac12\log_3(1/\varepsilon)\rceil$, $T=\lceil6/(m\varepsilon)\rceil$, and $0<\delta\le\min\{1/4,\varepsilon T/16\}$. Then both error terms in step 5.1 are at most $\varepsilon/2$, while $T+m3^m\le C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$: here $T=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$, $3^m=O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, and $m\varepsilon^{-1/2}=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$ because $\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^2$ is bounded on $(0,1/2)$. The sum $f_1+f_{2,\delta}$ is the required ReLU approximation.

citations.quote: Let a scalar-input ReLU network have $H\ge0$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_H$ and an affine output. On any interval, its output is affine on at most $\prod_{\ell=1}^H(n_\ell+1)$ subintervals. In particular, if it has $U=\sum_\ell n_\ell$ hidden units, the number of affine intervals is at most $(1+U/H)^H$ for $H\ge1$, and is $1$ when $H=0$.

derivations.claim: Since $f$ is nonlinear, its Hessian is nonzero at some interior point; otherwise all first derivatives are constant on the connected cube and $f$ is affine. Because the Hessian is symmetric, choose a direction $v$ with nonzero second directional derivative there. By continuity, after restricting to a sufficiently short line segment inside the cube and reparameterizing it by $t\in[0,1]$, the function $g(t)=f(x_0+tv)$ satisfies either $g''(t)\ge c_0>0$ throughout or $g''(t)\le-c_0<0$. Any network approximating $f$ within $\varepsilon$ restricts to a univariate network of the same depth and no more units.
Let $U$ be its number of hidden units and $H=L-2$. By [F1] and AM–GM, the restricted network has at most $M\le\prod_{\ell=1}^{H}(n_\ell+1)\le(1+U/H)^H$ affine intervals.

One of these intervals has length $h\ge1/M$. On it the network output $q$ is affine. If $g''\ge c_0$, then $g(a)+g(b)-2g((a+b)/2)\ge c_0h^2/4$; if $g''\le-c_0$, the negative of this second difference has the same lower bound. Since the second difference of $q$ is zero and each of the three approximation errors is at most $\varepsilon$, its magnitude for $g$ is at most $4\varepsilon$. Thus $\varepsilon\ge c_0h^2/16\ge c_0/(16M^2)$. Combining with step 2.1 yields $U\ge c(f,L)\varepsilon^{-1/(2H)}$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Each hidden unit has a bias parameter, so the number of weights is at least $U$ as well. This proves clause (iii).

derivations.claim: Let $R(m,d)$ be the largest possible number of complementary regions. With no hyperplanes or in dimension zero, $R(0,d)=R(m,0)=1$. Adding the last hyperplane $H$ splits only old regions that meet $H$; each old region is convex, so its intersection with $H$ contributes at most one region of the arrangement induced on $H\cong\mathbb R^{d-1}$. Hence $R(m,d)\le R(m-1,d)+R(m-1,d-1)$.

Induction on $m+d$ and Pascal's identity give $R(m,d)\le\sum_{j=0}^d\binom{m-1}{j}+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\binom{m-1}{j}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom mj$. If the arrangement is in general position, its restriction to $H$ is also in general position and has $m-1$ hyperplanes in dimension $d-1$; every one of its regions lies in one old region and cuts that region into two, so the recurrence is equality. Such arrangements exist: choose distinct $t_1,\ldots,t_m$ and use $H_i:\sum_{k=1}^d t_i^{k-1}x_k=t_i^d$. Any $q\le d$ normals are independent by the Vandermonde determinant, while no $d+1$ equations have a common solution because their augmented Vandermonde matrix is invertible. The same induction gives the claimed exact sum.

derivations.claim: On the current affine image, the $n_\ell$ preactivations are affine functions, so [F1] bounds the number of full-dimensional sign cells by $S=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(r,n_\ell)}\binom{n_\ell}{j}$. A sign cell has an active subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n_\ell\}$. By [F2], its output is the diagonal projection of the affine layer output that keeps coordinates in $A$ and sets the others to zero; its next affine image therefore has dimension at most $\min(r,|A|)$. Each subset labels at most one cell because its strict sign constraints are affine half-spaces on the current image.

Backward induction in the displayed recurrence shows that $R_{\ell+1}(s)$ is nondecreasing in $s$: increasing $s$ adds nonnegative terms and does not decrease any argument. Therefore, among at most $S$ distinct active subsets its sum is maximized by choosing the $S$ subsets of largest cardinality. Those can be taken to have sizes $n_\ell-j$ with multiplicities $\binom{n_\ell}{j}$ for $0\le j\le\min(r,n_\ell)$; their total number is exactly $S$. The associated next dimensions are at most $\min(r,n_\ell-j)$, giving the displayed recurrence. Induction backward from $R_{L+1}=1$ proves the claim.

derivations.claim: Set $t_0=0$, $t_{n+1}=1$, and $t_i=(2i-1)/(2n+1)$ for $1\le i\le n$. Put $y_i=0$ for even $i$ and $y_i=1$ for odd $i$, and define $s_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ for $0\le i\le n$. The piecewise-affine interpolant through $(t_i,y_i)$ maps every interval bijectively onto $[0,1]$. Its first slope is $s_0=2n+1$, while $s_2=(2n+1)/2$ and $s_3=-(2n+1)/2$, so $s_3-s_2=-s_0$.

Use hidden units $h_i(x)=\rho(x-t_i)$ for $i\ne3$ and $h_3(x)=\rho(t_3-x)$. Give unit $i$ output coefficient $a_i=s_i-s_{i-1}$, including $a_3=s_3-s_2=-s_0$, and set output bias $d=-a_3t_3$. Before $t_1$ only $h_3$ is active, so the output is $d+a_3(t_3-x)=s_0x$. At every $t_i$, the slope changes by $a_i$: for $i\ne3$ this is the right-facing ReLU slope jump, and for $i=3$ it is the left-facing ReLU slope jump. Thus the network output has the same initial value and slope jumps as the interpolant in step 1.1, so it equals that interpolant on $[0,1]$. This uses exactly $n$ hidden ReLU units and one affine output.

Each fold block's output is affine in the current hidden layer, so it can be substituted into the affine preactivations of the next adjacent layer without adding an intervening layer. At each knot $t_i$, exactly the corresponding hidden unit changes activation, so the $n+1$ intervals have distinct activation patterns. Each existing interval is cut into $n_{\ell+1}+1$ subintervals, each mapped bijectively onto $[0,1]$; the new layer's patterns distinguish these subintervals, while earlier layer patterns distinguish their parent intervals. Induction over the blocks gives $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$ intervals, each a distinct full-dimensional activation region.

citations.quote: For every integer $n\ge3$, there is a scalar-input standard adjacent-layer ReLU block with one hidden layer of width $n$ whose output is continuous and piecewise affine on $[0,1]$, has exactly $n$ interior breakpoints, and maps each of the resulting $n+1$ intervals bijectively onto $[0,1]$. Composing blocks of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge3$ yields $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$ full-dimensional activation regions in one input dimension.

Let $n_0,L,n_1,\ldots,n_L\ge1$ be integers and consider a standard adjacent-layer ReLU network with input dimension $n_0$ and $L$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_L$. Define $J$ to be the set of integer tuples $(j_1,\ldots,j_L)$ satisfying $$0\le j_\ell\le\min\{n_0,n_1-j_1,\ldots,n_{\ell-1}-j_{\ell-1},n_\ell\}\qquad(1\le\ell\le L),$$ where for $\ell=1$ the terms between $n_0$ and $n_\ell$ are absent. The number of full-dimensional activation-pattern regions is at most $$\sum_{(j_1,\ldots,j_L)\in J}\prod_{\ell=1}^L\binom{n_\ell}{j_\ell}.$$ For one hidden layer, the bound is attained by hyperplanes in general position.

For integers $m\ge0$ and $d\ge1$, the complement of any $m$ affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^d$ has at most $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom mj$ connected components, with $\binom mj=0$ for $j>m$. If the hyperplanes are in general position, meaning every $q\le d$ of them meet in codimension $q$ and no $d+1$ have a common point, the number of components is exactly this sum; such arrangements exist for every $m,d$. On a zero-dimensional affine image there is at most one full-dimensional activation cell.

derivations.claim: Compose the width-$n_\ell$ blocks from [F1]. Each existing interval is divided into $n_{\ell+1}+1$ intervals, each mapped onto $[0,1]$, so after all $L$ layers the number is $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(n_\ell+1)$.

For $n_0=1$, each index $j_\ell$ in [F2]'s upper sum is $0$ or $1$: the previous factors leave $n_i-j_i\ge2$ for every $n_i\ge3$. Thus the sum factors as $\prod_{\ell=1}^L(1+n_\ell)$, so the count in step 1.1 is exact. For the multidimensional construction, in each of the first $L-1$ layers allocate $q_\ell=\lfloor n_\ell/n_0\rfloor\ge3$ units to each coordinate and implement an independent width-$q_\ell$ fold on that coordinate; set any remaining units constantly inactive. Each prior box is thereby subdivided into $(q_\ell+1)^{n_0}$ boxes, each mapped bijectively onto $[0,1]^{n_0}$.

In the last hidden layer choose $n_L$ affine preactivation hyperplanes in general position in the image cube. By [F3], each of the boxes from step 2.1 has $\sum_{j=0}^{n_0}\binom{n_L}{j}$ activation cells in its preimage. Distinct boxes have disjoint interiors, so multiplying their counts gives the stated lower bound.

derivations.claim: Take independent Bernoulli variables $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ with success probability $x$, and put $S=\sum_iX_i$. The binomial formula gives $B_Nf(x)=\mathbb E f(S/N)$, so the Lipschitz hypothesis yields $|B_Nf(x)-f(x)|\le L\mathbb E|S/N-x|$.

Independence gives $\mathbb E S=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E X_i=Nx$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=Nx(1-x)$, because each Bernoulli variable has variance $x(1-x)$. Therefore Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\mathbb E|S/N-x|\le\sqrt{\mathbb E(S/N-x)^2}=\sqrt{x(1-x)/N}\le1/(2\sqrt N)$. The estimate holds for every $x$, proving the uniform bound.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,n\ge1$, let $Q=(0,1)^d$, and let $F_{d,n}$ be the unit ball of $W^{n,\infty}(Q;\mathbb R)$ for the norm given by the maximum of the essential suprema of all weak derivatives of order at most $n$. There is a constant $C=C(d,n)$ such that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ one can choose a ReLU network architecture, independent of $f\in F_{d,n}$, for which every $f\in F_{d,n}$ has weights producing a representative $\Phi_f$ with $$\|f-\Phi_f\|_{L^\infty(Q)}\le\varepsilon,$$ depth at most $C(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$, and at most $C\varepsilon^{-d/n}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ weights and computation units.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F_{1,1}$ be the unit ball of $W^{1,\infty}((0,1);\mathbb R)$ under the maximum norm of the function and its weak derivative, using the Lipschitz representative on $[0,1]$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $f\in F_{1,1}$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, an architecture depending on $f$ computes a ReLU approximation with uniform error at most $\varepsilon$, depth $6$ counting input and output layers, and at most $C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$ weights, connections, and computation units.

derivations.claim: The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x)=x$, so $\|f\|_{L^\infty}=1/2$ and $\|f'\|_{L^\infty}=1$. By [F1], $\|f\|_{W^{1,\infty}}=1$. Directly, $|x^2-y^2|/2=|x-y||x+y|/2\le|x-y|$ on $[0,1]$, so $f$ is unit-Lipschitz.

Apply [F2] and [F3] to this same target. Their size ratio is $[1/(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))]/[\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon)]=(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2}$ up to constants, which tends to zero. This compares existence rates only and makes no claim about optimization or training.

Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network from $[0,1]^d$ to $\mathbb R^r$ is a finite acyclic feedforward computation graph with $d$ input coordinates, hidden units applying $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to affine combinations of earlier unit values, and $r$ affine output units. Edges may skip layers. Its depth is the maximum number of layers met on an input-to-output path, counting the input and output layers, so a network with one hidden layer has depth $3$. Its computation units are its hidden and output units; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. The number of each quantity counts scalar entries, including zero entries only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network is the specialization in which edges join consecutive layers and every such edge is present.
